title: Industrial Case Study 2: Real-Time Collaborative Streaming Engine
goal: How do platforms like Figma, Google Docs, or Slack synchronize live updates across hundreds of thousands of users in real time? Today, we architect a Real-Time Collaborative Streaming Engine. Because WebSocket connections are persistent TCP sockets bound to specific gateway pods, horizontally scaling across a Kubernetes cluster requires a distributed Pub/Sub message broker (Redis Pub/Sub) to bridge isolated memory spaces. Master distributed socket connection routing, understand the quadratic message explosion physics of collaborative canvases, implement cursor coordinate throttling, and build resilient sliding-window reconnection buffers to guarantee sub-20ms broadcast latency under high concurrency!
recap: Yesterday in Day 56, we architected a mission-critical High-Frequency Fintech Transactional Ledger with exact decimal precision, double-entry bookkeeping, serializable concurrency, and cryptographic audit hashing.

parts.example: Calculating message explosion physics: 1,000 active users at 60 FPS generates 60 million messages/sec without throttling.
parts.code:
def calculate_broadcast_load(users: int, fps: int):
    raw_msgs_per_sec = users * (users - 1) * fps
    return raw_msgs_per_sec

unthrottled = calculate_broadcast_load(users=1000, fps=60)
throttled = calculate_broadcast_load(users=1000, fps=10)

print(f"1,000 Users @ 60 FPS: {unthrottled:,} msgs/sec (CRITICAL OVERLOAD!)")
print(f"1,000 Users @ 10 FPS (Throttled): {throttled:,} msgs/sec")
print(f"Load Reduction: {((unthrottled - throttled) / unthrottled * 100):.1f}%")
print("Explosion Invariant: Ingress throttling eliminates quadratic pub/sub CPU saturation.")
parts.output:
1,000 Users @ 60 FPS: 59,940,000 msgs/sec (CRITICAL OVERLOAD!)
1,000 Users @ 10 FPS (Throttled): 9,990,000 msgs/sec
Load Reduction: 83.3%
Explosion Invariant: Ingress throttling eliminates quadratic pub/sub CPU saturation.
codeNotes: Unthrottled collaborative broadcasting scales quadratically as O(N^2), causing CPU saturation under large room sizes.
Throttling cursor frequency to 10-15 FPS drops message volume by over 80% while preserving a smooth user perception.

check.question: What is the time complexity of naive message broadcasting in a collaborative room with N participants?
options: O(N^2) quadratic scaling, because every participant emits events that must be fanned out to all other N - 1 participants.
O(1) constant scaling, because Redis broadcasts all messages instantaneously.
O(log N) logarithmic scaling, because modern WebSockets use binary tree socket trees.
O(N) linear scaling, because TCP packets are multiplexed automatically by the kernel.
check.why: With N users each emitting updates to N-1 peers, the total message throughput scales quadratically as N * (N - 1), creating extreme load.

parts.title: Resilient Collaborative Reconnection & State Catch-Up
say: In real-world networks, mobile devices frequently switch between Wi-Fi and 5G cellular networks, dropping active TCP connections. In mobile and distributed environments, transient network disconnects are inevitable; collaborative platforms must provide seamless reconnection and state recovery. Production architectures maintain strict observability across all distributed nodes. Production architectures maintain strict observability across all distributed nodes. When a user's WebSocket reconnects after a 3-second network blip, transferring the entire multi-megabyte document state from scratch creates terrible lag. The streaming engine maintains an in-memory sliding window ring buffer of recent document operations, tagging every edit with a monotonically increasing sequence number. Instead, an industrial collaborative engine maintains an in-memory sliding-window operation buffer tagged with monotonically increasing sequence numbers. When a disconnected client reconnects, it supplies its last acknowledged sequence number, allowing the hub to stream the missing delta operations rather than resending the full document. When reconnecting, the client sends its last acknowledged sequence number (e.g., seq=2). The server inspects its ring buffer and replays only the missing delta operations. If a client has been disconnected too long and the ring buffer has expired, the hub seamlessly falls back to streaming a fresh snapshot of the authoritative state.
